    The Bokut–Shiao completion, and the fact that the counterexample is the missing rule #

    HeckeGS.lean §4e refutes hecke_is_gs_basis: at n = 4 the overlap of the Yang–Baxter rule for (σ₂, σ₃) with the far-commutation rule for (σ₃, σ₁), over the ambient word σ₃σ₂σ₃σ₁, has S-polynomial

    σ₂σ₃σ₂σ₁ − σ₃σ₂σ₁σ₃

    and both words are irreducible for heckeRewritingSystem. That module also says what is missing — Bokut & Shiao complete the presentation with the family

    σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ ⋯ σⱼ σᵢ → σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ ⋯ σⱼ (j ≤ i − 1)

    This file makes that family a definition and checks the claim that connects the two: the refuting S-polynomial is, up to sign, exactly the missing rule at (i, j) = (3, 1). bsWord₁ 3 1 = σ₃σ₂σ₁σ₃ and bsWord₂ 2 3 1 = σ₂σ₃σ₂σ₁ are precisely NotAGSBasis.w₂ and NotAGSBasis.w₁. So for the completed system the S-polynomial is no longer a normal form (spoly_not_isNormalForm_completed), and the specific obstruction §4e exhibits is gone.

    The family carries no q #

    Unlike the quadratic relation, the Bokut–Shiao words need no deformation: the identity is a braid-group identity, provable from the braid and far-commutation relations alone, with the quadratic relation never used. Two lines, in the algebra:

    σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ ⋯ σⱼ σᵢ = σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ σᵢ₋₂ ⋯ σⱼ (σᵢ commutes past σᵢ₋₂ … σⱼ) = σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ₋₂ ⋯ σⱼ (braid)

    so the rule is the same two-term shape as yangBaxterRelation, which it subsumes at j = i − 1.

    Indices #

    bokutShiaoRelation takes i', i, j with i' standing for i − 1, related by the side condition i'.val + 1 = i.val carried on the enumeration rather than by Fin arithmetic. That keeps every word here free of subtraction and every membership proof in the same flatMap/filterMap shape the existing system uses.

    What is established here #

    Both of the harder statements this section once listed as open are now proved. Read this list, not a memory of it — the heading said "what is not established" long after the second item had landed 18,663 lines below, with the first already marked DONE, and a reader who stopped here concluded the opposite of what the file proves (bean qou-nk5h).

    • The general leading monomial (§4h). bokutShiaoRelation_lm : lm (bokutShiaoRelation i' i j) = bsWord₁ i j, via descWord_cons : descWord i j = ⟨i⟩ :: descWord i' j. As predicted, no length computation was needed: the cons lemma gives both words a visible common tail (σᵢ :: (w ++ [σᵢ]) against σᵢ₋₁ :: σᵢ :: w, same w), so the lengths agree by simp and the comparison is one List.Lex.rel on the first letter. descWord_cons reduces to a statement about List.finRange n being Pairwise (· < ·): once the head is i every later index exceeds it and both filters annihilate the tail, and before the head is reached the two predicates agree because a < i = i' + 1 forces a ≤ i'.
    • The completed system IS a Gröbner–Shirshov basis (§4bw). heckeCompleted_isGrobnerShirshovBasis, unconditional, for every n and every HeckeParams. This was the harder half — it needed the overlap analysis re-run against the completed rule set, a strictly larger set of compositions since the new family overlaps itself, and resolving the §4e overlap alone was necessary but not sufficient. The remaining hdeep obligation of heckeCompleted_isGrobnerShirshovBasis_of_deep (§4bn) is discharged by deep_selfOverlap_resolves (§4bw).

    What is still assumed #

    One thing, and it is not the criterion above:

    • The Diamond Lemma. heckeCompleted_normalForm_unique and heckeCompleted_threading_cost_unique (§4bx) route through normal_form_unique, which rides on the axioms reduction_well_founded (Basic.lean) and local_confluence (CompositionLemma.lean, Bergman 1978 §3 Thm 1.2). So unique normal forms at every n holds given the Diamond Lemma; the GS-basis criterion itself does not depend on either axiom.

    Beans qou-auq3, qou-nk5h.

                The S-polynomial's coefficient at w₂ #

                §4e proves spoly.coeff w₁ = 1. The other word carries −1, by the mirror argument: the Yang–Baxter half of the S-polynomial has shape _ ++ [σ₁] and w₂ ends in σ₃, so that half contributes nothing; the far-commutation half has shape [σ₃, σ₂] ++ _ and contributes σ₁σ₃'s coefficient, which is −1.

                The completed system reduces the S-polynomial that refutes the uncompleted one. w₂ carries a non-zero coefficient and is the leading monomial of bs31, hence an infix of itself — so the S-polynomial is not a normal form, and the obstruction of §4e is gone.

                Contrast NotAGSBasis.spoly_isNormalForm, which is the same S-polynomial against heckeRewritingSystem.

                The refuting overlap resolves in the completed system #

                spoly_not_isNormalForm_completed says only that the S-polynomial is no longer irreducible. The Gröbner–Shirshov condition asks for more — that it reduces to zero — and here it does, in a single step, for a reason worth seeing:

                oc.spoly       =  w₁ − w₂        (§4e: coeff w₁ = 1, coeff w₂ = −1)
bs31.relation  =  w₂ − w₁        (bsWord₁ 3 1 = w₂, bsWord₂ 2 3 1 = w₁)

                They are negatives of each other. So one application of bs31 in empty context with coefficient −1 annihilates it exactly. The obstruction and its repair are the same two words with opposite signs.

                §4h The general leading monomial #

                The cons lemma the module docstring names as the one thing missing. With it, bokutShiaoRelation_lm needs no length computation: both words acquire a visible common tail and the deg-lex comparison is one List.Lex.rel on the first letter.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.filter_desc_cons {n : ℕ} {i' i j : Fin n} (hi : ↑i' + 1 = ↑i) (hj : ↑j ≤ ↑i') (l : List (Fin n)) :
                List.Pairwise (fun (a b : Fin n) => ↑a < ↑b) l → i ∈ l → List.filter (fun (k : Fin n) => decide (↑j ≤ ↑k ∧ ↑k ≤ ↑i)) l = List.filter (fun (k : Fin n) => decide (↑j ≤ ↑k ∧ ↑k ≤ ↑i')) l ++ [i]

                List.finRange n is Pairwise (· < ·), so once the head is i every later index exceeds it and both filters annihilate the tail; before the head is reached the two predicates agree, because a < i = i' + 1 forces a ≤ i'.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.descWord_cons {n : ℕ} {i' i j : Fin n} (hi : ↑i' + 1 = ↑i) (hj : ↑j ≤ ↑i') :
                descWord i j = { index := i } :: descWord i' j

                The cons lemma: dropping the top index drops the first letter.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.bsWord₁_cons {n : ℕ} {i' i j : Fin n} (hi : ↑i' + 1 = ↑i) (hj : ↑j ≤ ↑i') :
                bsWord₁ i j = { index := i } :: (descWord i' j ++ [{ index := i }])

                Both Bokut–Shiao words in cons form, sharing a visible tail. This is what makes the leading-monomial comparison a one-letter lex step with no length arithmetic: σᵢ :: (w ++ [σᵢ]) against σᵢ₋₁ :: σᵢ :: w, same w.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.bokutShiaoRelation_lm {n : ℕ} {i' i j : Fin n} (hi : ↑i' + 1 = ↑i) (hj : ↑j ≤ ↑i') :
                (bokutShiaoRelation i' i j).lm (heckeOrder n) = bsWord₁ i j

                The general leading monomial lm(bokutShiaoRelation i' i j) = bsWord₁ i j.

                Both words have length |descWord i' j| + 2 — visible from bsWord₁_cons, with no length computation — and deg-lex ranks σᵢ above σᵢ₋₁, so the word starting with σᵢ is the larger. Compare Completion.bs31_lm, which is this at (i', i, j) = (2, 3, 1) and was proved by fin_cases before this existed.

                §4j The family subsumes Yang–Baxter #

                At j = i − 1 the Bokut–Shiao words are the braid words. So the completed system's Yang–Baxter rules are not new information relative to the family — which matters for the overlap analysis ahead, since it means YB × BS overlaps are a special case of BS × BS rather than a separate family to enumerate.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.filter_desc_self {n : ℕ} (i : Fin n) (l : List (Fin n)) :
                List.Pairwise (fun (a b : Fin n) => ↑a < ↑b) l → i ∈ l → List.filter (fun (k : Fin n) => decide (↑i ≤ ↑k ∧ ↑k ≤ ↑i)) l = [i]

                The filter that defines descWord i i keeps exactly the one index i: everything after i in a Pairwise (· < ·) list exceeds it, and everything before it is below. Same shape as filter_desc_cons.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.descWord_self {n : ℕ} (i : Fin n) :
                descWord i i = [{ index := i }]

                The descending word from i down to i is the single letter σᵢ.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.bsWord₁_at_pred {n : ℕ} {i' i : Fin n} (hi : ↑i' + 1 = ↑i) :
                bsWord₁ i i' = [{ index := i }, { index := i' }, { index := i }]

                At j = i − 1 the left Bokut–Shiao word is the braid word σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.bsWord₂_at_pred {n : ℕ} (i' i : Fin n) :
                bsWord₂ i' i i' = [{ index := i' }, { index := i }, { index := i' }]

                …and the right one is σᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁.

                Note this needs no relation between i' and i: bsWord₂ i' i j is σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ followed by descWord i' j, so at j = i' the tail collapses by descWord_self whatever i is. It is the left word that needs i' + 1 = i, because that is where descWord_cons is used.

                source
                theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.bokutShiaoRelation_at_pred {n : ℕ} {i' i : Fin n} (hi : ↑i' + 1 = ↑i) :
                (bokutShiaoRelation i' i i').relation = AlgElement.ofTerms [([{ index := i }, { index := i' }, { index := i }], 1), ([{ index := i' }, { index := i }, { index := i' }], -1)]

                The Bokut–Shiao rule at j = i − 1 is the Yang–Baxter rule, up to the sign convention: its relation is σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ − σᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁, and yangBaxterRelation i' i is the negative of that.

                So the family really does extend the presentation rather than sit beside it, and the two rules share a leading monomial (bokutShiao_lm_eq_yangBaxter_lm).

                source

                (bokutShiaoRelation i' i i').lm (heckeOrder n) = (yangBaxterRelation i' i).lm (heckeOrder n)

                Both rules lead on σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ — deg-lex ranks σᵢ above σᵢ₋₁, so the word starting with the larger generator wins, exactly as in yangBaxterRelation_lm.

                §4i Every rule of the completed system, classified #

                The analogue of heckeRewritingSystem_lm_cases for the completed system. That classification is what §4e's irreducibility machinery runs on — no_rule_infix_w₁ and friends dispatch on it — so the completed system needs its own before any of that can be redone against it.

                Two levels, and the difference between them is load-bearing here in a way it is not for the uncompleted system. mem_heckeCompletedRewritingSystem_rules inverts membership to the rule; heckeCompletedRewritingSystem_lm_cases inverts it only as far as the rule's leading monomial, and is now a corollary of the first. §4j is exactly the reason the weaker one cannot stand in for the stronger: bokutShiao_lm_eq_yangBaxter_lm puts bokutShiaoRelation i' i i' and yangBaxterRelation i' i on one leading monomial, so in this system the lm does not determine the rule. Anything phrased through OverlapComposition.spoly — which is computed from rule.relation and rule.lc — therefore needs the rule-level inversion; the criterion's overlap_resolves is such a statement.

                No rule of the completed system has an empty leading monomial — the non-degeneracy gs_basis_of_empty_lm shows is essential, re-established for the larger rule set. The Bokut–Shiao words are never empty: bsWord₁ i j ends in σᵢ.

                §4k The overlap set of the completed system, enumerated #

                §4g resolves one overlap. Completeness needs every one of them, and until now "how many are there" was prose: four families, and the new family overlaps itself — a shape, not a number. This section produces the number.

                An OverlapComposition is pinned by three words: lm₁ = left ++ overlap, lm₂ = overlap ++ right, overlap ≠ []. The rules never enter, only their leading monomials — so once those are a list, the overlap shapes are a computation, and mem_overlapTriples is the bridge carrying any composition of the completed system into that list.

                Two rules with the same leading monomial give the same shape, and §4j says that is not hypothetical: at j = i − 1 the Bokut–Shiao and Yang–Baxter rules lead on the same word. completedLMSet deduplicates, so overlapTriples counts shapes; the rule-level multiplicity at those three words is a separate question.

                At n = 4 the numbers are 16 rules, 13 distinct leading monomials, 58 overlap shapes — of which 13 are the degenerate lm₁ = lm₂ self-pairings with both contexts empty and 45 have both contexts non-empty. NotAGSBasis.oc is one of the 45.

                              §4l The degenerate shapes resolve #

                              Thirteen of the fifty-eight shapes are degenerate: both contexts empty, the two rules leading on the same word. They are still proof obligations — OverlapComposition admits them — and they split in two.

                              When the two rules coincide the S-polynomial is the difference of an element with itself: OverlapComposition.spoly_isZero_of_self, proved in the framework because nothing about it is Hecke-specific.

                                      §4m Two structural facts, and what they leave #

                                      Both decided by the kernel at n = 4. Together they say the remaining work has a much narrower shape than the enumeration alone suggests.

                                      Every proper overlap is a single letter. Not one of the forty-five non-degenerate shapes overlaps in two or more generators. The reason is visible in the four families: every leading monomial is descending after its first letter (σᵢσᵢ, σⱼσᵢσⱼ with j = i+1, σᵢσⱼ with j < i, and bsWord₁), so a suffix of length ≥ 2 ends low-then-high while every prefix of length ≥ 2 starts high-then-low. Only a single letter can be both. Every composition is therefore "lm₁ ends with x, lm₂ begins with x" — one shared generator.

                                      The leading monomials form an infix antichain: none is a proper factor of another. This is the stronger statement, and it settles the inclusion half of IsGrobnerShirshovBasis structurally — inclusion_contexts_empty below shows every inclusion composition of the completed system has both contexts empty, with no hypothesis about which rules are involved. The inclusion half is then exactly the shared-leading-monomial case, which DegenerateYbBs and InclusionComposition.spoly_isZero_of_self between them handle.

                                      What is left after this section is the forty-five proper overlap shapes, minus the one #4879 resolved.

                                        Why it resolves. Write out the S-polynomial:

                                        lc₂ • (BS · σ_{j₀}) − lc₁ • (descWord i j · FC)
  = (bsWord₁ i j ++ [σ_{j₀}] − bsWord₂ i' i j ++ [σ_{j₀}])
    − (descWord i j ++ [σᵢ, σ_{j₀}] − descWord i j ++ [σ_{j₀}, σᵢ])

                                        descWord i j ++ [σ_{j₀}] ++ [σᵢ] = descWord i j₀ ++ [σᵢ] = bsWord₁ i j₀
bsWord₂ i' i j ++ [σ_{j₀}]                                = bsWord₂ i' i j₀

                                            §4p Any two-term rule against the quadratic rule — one family, three steps #

                                            §4n and §4o each resolve a composition in no steps or one. This is the first family that needs a genuine reduction chain, and it is the largest single block left: twelve of the n = 4 shapes, and again general in n.

                                            The observation that makes it one family. Every two-term rule of the completed system has its two words in cyclic position — the leading monomial is u' ++ [σₓ] and the other word is σ_y :: u', the same u' in both:

                                            farCommRelation i j      u' = [σᵢ]              x = j    y = j

bokutShiaoRelation i' i j  u' = descWord i j    x = i    y = i−1

                                            (the last because descWord i j = σᵢ :: descWord i₋₁ j, so bsWord₂ i' i j = σᵢ₋₁ :: descWord i j.) Nothing else about the rule is used.

                                            The chain. The leading monomial ends in σₓ, so it overlaps σₓσₓ in that one letter, over u' ++ [σₓ, σₓ]. The ambient word cancels and

                                            spoly = −(σ_y :: u' ++ [σₓ]) + h·(u' ++ [σₓ]) + u'      (times `c`)

                                            Then, in three steps:

                                            2. which begins σ_yσ_y, so the quadratic rule at y applies — a different generator from the one the composition is about, which is why this needs a chain rather than a single annihilation — leaving h·(σ_y :: u') + u';
                                            3. what is left is h times r's own relation, killed by r in empty context.

                                            Step 3 needs h ≠ 0, and that is where HeckeParams finally earns its q > 0 ∧ q ≠ 1: the composition does not resolve at q = 1.

                                                §4r The braid self-overlap σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ #

                                                The single largest block of what remains at n = 4: twelve of the forty compositions, and the classical one — the braid relation overlapping itself.

                                                Three words carry it (σ₁σ₀σ₁σ₀σ₁, σ₂σ₁σ₂σ₁σ₂, σ₃σ₂σ₃σ₂σ₃) and each carries two rules with the same leading monomial (§4j: Yang–Baxter, and Bokut–Shiao at j = i − 1), so four ordered rule-pairs per word. Stating the family for an abstract pair r₁, r₂ — each with leading monomial σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ and relation c·σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ − c·σᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁ — covers all twelve at once, and generally in n.

                                                The S-polynomial is two terms. Both rules lead on the ambient word, so it cancels and nothing about c₁, c₂ survives except their product:

                                                spoly = c₁c₂ · ( σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁  −  σᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₁σᵢ )

                                                The chain is eight steps, derived from the n = 4 confluence engine and recorded here because it is the specification the remaining proof has to meet. Writing I = σᵢ, J = σᵢ₋₁, and K = c₁c₂:

                                                # target rule context coefficient
                                                1 IJJIJ Q_{i-1} (I ∣ IJ) K
                                                2 JIJJI Q_{i-1} (JI ∣ I) −K
                                                3 IJIJ r₁ (ε ∣ J) K·h·c₁
                                                4 JIJI r₁ (J ∣ ε) −K·h·c₁
                                                5 JIJJ Q_{i-1} (JI ∣ ε) K·h
                                                6 JJIJ Q_{i-1} (ε ∣ IJ) −K·h
                                                7 IIJ Q_i (ε ∣ J) K
                                                8 JII Q_i (J ∣ ε) −K

                                                Four applications of the quadratic rule at i − 1, two of the braid rule itself, two of the quadratic rule at i. No intermediate exceeds five terms, and h² appears in exactly one of them (F₅) before cancelling. Steps 3 and 4 need c₁ · c₁ = 1 — both instances have c = ±1 — because the step coefficient must satisfy c₃ · lc(r₁) = K·h and lc(r₁) = c₁.

                                                h ≠ 0 is needed for steps 3–6, as in §4p and §4q.

                                                                      Bokut–Shiao against Bokut–Shiao.

                                                                      §4s Bokut–Shiao against far-commutation at the same index #

                                                                      §4o did j₀ + 1 = j — the far-commutation rule extending the descending run by one step, which resolves in a single application. This is the neighbouring case j₀ = j, where the two rules share their bottom index. It does not resolve in one step: the shared index puts σⱼσⱼ at the end of both words, so the quadratic rule fires twice before the Bokut–Shiao rules can.

                                                                      Writing jp for j + 1 and using descWord_snoc (§4o) — descWord i j = descWord i jp ++ [σⱼ], and hence bsWord₂ i' i j = bsWord₂ i' i jp ++ [σⱼ] — the S-polynomial is

                                                                      (descWord i jp ++ [σⱼ, σⱼ, σᵢ])  −  (bsWord₂ i' i jp ++ [σⱼ, σⱼ])

                                                                      and both terms end in σⱼσⱼ. Four steps:

                                                                      # target rule context coefficient
                                                                      1 the first term Q_j (descWord i jp ∣ σᵢ) 1
                                                                      2 the second Q_j (bsWord₂ i' i jp ∣ ε) −1
                                                                      3 bsWord₁ i j Bokut–Shiao at j (ε ∣ ε) h
                                                                      4 bsWord₁ i jp Bokut–Shiao at jp (ε ∣ ε) 1

                                                                      Steps 3 and 4 use the family's own rules at two adjacent depths — the h term the two squares leave behind is the Bokut–Shiao relation at j, the constant term is the one at jp. That is the same downward self-completion §4o exhibited, arriving here through the quadratic rule rather than directly.

                                                                      Where the side condition comes from. Step 4 needs bokutShiaoRelation i' i jp to be a rule, that is j + 1 ≤ i − 1 — which is exactly the condition for σᵢσⱼ to be a far-commutation word in the first place, so nothing is left over. At j = i − 1 there is no composition to resolve: σᵢσᵢ₋₁ is a braid word, not a commuting pair, and that case is §4r's. At n = 4 this family is three compositions, (i', i, j) ∈ {(1,2,0), (2,3,0), (2,3,1)}.

                                                                      Every word in the chain is descWord i jp prefixed or suffixed, and the single fact that tells the two sides apart is the first letter — σᵢ on the bsWord₁ side (because descWord i jp begins with σᵢ), σᵢ₋₁ on the bsWord₂ side. head_ne is that observation, and apart from one length count it is the only word-distinctness the chain needs.

                                                                                §4t The quadratic rule against a general Bokut–Shiao rule #

                                                                                §4q covers the quadratic rule on the left against far-commutation, Yang–Baxter, and Bokut–Shiao at j = i − 1 — everything whose second word has the cyclic shape u'' ++ [σ_z]. It says explicitly why the general Bokut–Shiao rule is not among them: bsWord₂ i' i j = σᵢ₋₁ :: descWord i j puts the extra letter on the left, so for j < i − 1 no σ_z closes the cycle. This section is those missing instances — three of the ninety-two at n = 4, and the first family in this arc whose chain length is not constant.

                                                                                The shape. With v for descWord i−2 j, so that descWord i' j = σᵢ₋₁ :: v, the two words of the rule are

                                                                                bsWord₁ i j = σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ v σᵢ        bsWord₂ i' i j = σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ v

                                                                                and the composition is Q_i against it over σᵢ σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ v σᵢ. The S-polynomial is three terms,

                                                                                spoly = σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ σᵢ₋₁ v  −  h · bsWord₁ i j  −  σᵢ₋₁ v σᵢ

                                                                                The chain is 3 + |v| steps, and only the first three are fixed:

                                                                                # target rule context coefficient
                                                                                1 σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁v Yang–Baxter (ε ∣ σᵢ₋₁ v) −1
                                                                                2 σᵢ₋₁σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₁v Q_{i−1} (σᵢ₋₁σᵢ ∣ v) 1
                                                                                3 bsWord₁ i j Bokut–Shiao at j (ε ∣ ε) −h
                                                                                4… — far-commutation — 1

                                                                                Step 1 straightens the braid, step 2 squares out the σᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₁ that leaves, and step 3 spends the h term against the rule's own relation. What remains is

                                                                                σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ v  −  σᵢ₋₁ v σᵢ

                                                                                — one letter σᵢ on the wrong side of v, and every letter of v has index at most i − 2, so each is a far-commutation letter for σᵢ. The rest of the chain walks σᵢ across v one letter at a time and the two terms cancel. That is |v| = i − 1 − j steps, giving 3 + (i−1−j) in total — the 4, 4, 5 the n = 4 confluence engine reports for Q2 × B120, Q3 × B231, Q3 × B230.

                                                                                          §4u Far-commutation on the left, against Bokut–Shiao or Yang–Baxter #

                                                                                          §4o, §4s and §4t all have the far-commutation rule on the right of the composition. This is the other side: farCommRelation x m leads on σₓσ_m, a Bokut–Shiao or Yang–Baxter rule leads on a word beginning with σ_m, and the two overlap in that single letter.

                                                                                          The shape. Write the second rule as c · (σ_m :: u'') − c · w₂ — leading monomial σ_m :: u'', other word w₂, monic up to c. Both Bokut–Shiao and Yang–Baxter are of this form, and at j = i − 1 both rules sit on the same leading monomial (§4j), which is why this section proves two instances rather than one. The ambient word σₓ σ_m u'' cancels and

                                                                                          spoly = c · (σₓ :: w₂)  −  c · (σ_m :: σₓ :: u'')

                                                                                          Why it resolves, and why it is a transport. σₓ commutes far with every letter of the second rule, because m + 1 < x is the far-commutation side condition and every letter of w₂ and of u'' has index at most m. So σₓ is a passenger in both terms, and the chain simply walks it to the right end of each:

                                                                                          phase term steps
                                                                                          1 σₓ :: w₂ → w₂ ++ [σₓ] \|w₂\|
                                                                                          2 σ_m :: σₓ :: u'' → σ_m :: (u'' ++ [σₓ]) \|u''\|
                                                                                          3 the rule itself, in the context (ε ∣ σₓ) 1

                                                                                          After phase 2 the second term is (σ_m :: u'') ++ [σₓ] — the rule's leading monomial with σₓ appended — so one application of the rule in the context (ε ∣ σₓ) turns it into w₂ ++ [σₓ] and the two terms cancel. Total |w₂| + |u''| + 1, which is 6 for both n = 4 instances.

                                                                                          Why the transport needs a passenger. farComm_transport (§4t) moves a generator across a word in an element whose other term is the transport's own destination, so the two cancel at the end. Here the other term is a bystander: it has to be carried along untouched, and the step's "targeted coefficient is non-zero" condition needs it distinguished from every intermediate word. Hence farComm_transport_snd and farComm_transport_fst — the same induction with the bystander in the second and the first list slot. Both slots are genuinely needed: each phase transports a different term, so whichever slot phase 1 leaves the moving term in, phase 2 needs the other one.

                                                                                                  §4v Bokut–Shiao or Yang–Baxter against far-commutation below the run #

                                                                                                  The third and last regime of BS/YB × farCommRelation i j₀. §4o is j₀ + 1 = j (one step: the S-polynomial is the Bokut–Shiao rule one index lower) and §4s is j₀ = j (four steps: a square at each end). This is j₀ + 1 < j, where σ_{j₀} sits strictly below the whole descending run and therefore commutes past all of it. The S-polynomial is

                                                                                                  spoly = c · (descWord i j ++ [σ_{j₀}, σᵢ])  −  c · (w₂ ++ [σ_{j₀}])

                                                                                                  writing the first rule as c · bsWord₁ i j − c · w₂, and both terms have a stray σ_{j₀} that wants to be at the front:

                                                                                                  phase term steps
                                                                                                  1 descWord i j σ_{j₀} σᵢ → σ_{j₀} descWord i j σᵢ \|descWord i j\|
                                                                                                  2 w₂ σ_{j₀} → σ_{j₀} w₂ \|w₂\|
                                                                                                  3 the rule, in the context (σ_{j₀} ∣ ε) 1

                                                                                                  After phase 1 the first term is σ_{j₀} :: bsWord₁ i j, so one application of the rule in the context (σ_{j₀} ∣ ε) turns it into σ_{j₀} :: w₂ and the terms cancel. Six steps for both n = 4 instances.

                                                                                                  This is the mirror transport, and it is a different lemma. §4t and §4u move a big generator rightwards through small ones; here a small generator moves leftwards through big ones. Same rule σ_aσ_b → σ_bσ_a, opposite role in it: the moving letter is the second factor of the leading monomial rather than the first, so the induction recurses at the other end of the word and needs a right context, which neither earlier transport carries.

                                                                                                  farComm_transport_left is therefore stated once, in a form that also removes the list-slot duplication §4u had to live with: the moving term sits at an arbitrary position L₁ ++ (·) :: L₂ of the ofTerms list, so one lemma serves both phases. ofTerms_coeff_mid is what makes that work — the coefficient of a singled-out term, given that no other term carries its word.

                                                                                                  Where the last regime went. j < j₀ (the n = 4 composition B230 × F31) is not this: σ_{j₀} lands inside the run's index range, so it does not commute past σ_{j₀±1}, and the chain instead fires the Bokut–Shiao rule at the inner index j₀ first. That one is left.

                                                                                                  §4ak A cancelling pair drops out #

                                                                                                  The a ≤ b chain's term list is not fixed-shape. hecke_chain_cancellation.py measures its profile: the two quadratic steps each add a term (peak four), and then two later steps remove two at once — which no rewrite can do, since a far-commutation takes one term to one term. Each is a pair reconverging on a single word with opposite coefficients and annihilating. Worked at a = 4, b = 6, step 24 rewrites h · σ_i σ_{i−4} ⋯ into precisely the word already carried by −h, and the two vanish.

                                                                                                  The first such event is mid-prefix; the second is the final step, so the chain does not terminate by a separate mechanism — reaching zero is itself a cancellation. That is why the lemma below is needed twice, and why the second use is what will deliver "reduces to zero".

                                                                                                  MultiStepReduction is stated through CoeffEq, so the cancellation is sound with no help at all (§6 already carries the congruences). What is missing is the shape bridge: without it every lemma downstream of a cancellation would have to be stated against a list whose first two entries are dead weight.

                                                                                                  Two terms on one word with opposite coefficients contribute nothing, even with other terms between them.

                                                                                                  The adjacent case is what §4ak's cancellations need at the top level; the a ≤ b closing phase needs the split one. There the four-term element is [(Vh, h), (V1, 1), (Uh, −h), (U1, −1)], and the two terms that reconverge are the two h-weighted ones — with (V1, 1) sitting between them. That ordering is not a choice: trio emits its h-weighted word immediately before its plain one, in place, so the two lineages interleave as V, V, U, U.

                                                                                                  ofTerms_cancel_pair is this at M = [].

                                                                                                  The induction recurses on the head of w and appends its step at the end, which is the opposite end from farComm_transport: there the moving letter leads, here it trails. In the corner chain of §4af the bystanding term is the final word, so the unrestricted hypothesis is false exactly where the transport is needed. farComm_transport_left below is this with the stronger hypothesis, kept because §4v's callers already supply it.

                                                                                                          §4w Far-commutation inside the descending run — the last regime #

                                                                                                          The fourth and last position j₀ can take relative to descWord i j, and the one that is not a transport. §4o (j₀ + 1 = j), §4s (j₀ = j) and §4v (j₀ + 1 < j) all have σ_{j₀} at or below the bottom of the run. Here j < j₀, so σ_{j₀} is a letter the run already contains, and it does not commute past its own neighbours σ_{j₀±1}.

                                                                                                          What happens instead. Split the run at j₀:

                                                                                                          descWord i j = descWord i jup ++ (σ_{j₀} :: descWord j₀' j)

                                                                                                          writing jup for j₀ + 1 and j₀' for j₀ − 1. Then the first term of the S-polynomial ends in

                                                                                                          descWord j₀ j ++ [σ_{j₀}]  =  bsWord₁ j₀ j

                                                                                                          — the Bokut–Shiao word at the inner index j₀. So the inner rule fires first, and what it leaves is σ_{j₀'} :: σ_{j₀} :: descWord j₀' j, whose leading σ_{j₀'} is now below everything above it and can be transported to the front. The same thing happens in the second term. Five stages:

                                                                                                          # target rule context
                                                                                                          1 bsWord₁ j₀ j in term 1 Bokut–Shiao at j₀ (σᵢ descWord i' jup ∣ σᵢ)
                                                                                                          2… σ_{j₀'} to the front far-commutation \|descWord i jup\| steps
                                                                                                          3 bsWord₁ j₀ j in term 2 Bokut–Shiao at j₀ (σᵢ₋₁σᵢ descWord i' jup ∣ ε)
                                                                                                          4… σ_{j₀'} to the front far-commutation \|descWord i' jup\| + 2 steps

                                                                                                          After stage 2 the first term is σ_{j₀'} :: bsWord₁ i j and after stage 4 the second is σ_{j₀'} :: bsWord₂ i' i j, so the outer rule in the context (σ_{j₀'} ∣ ε) closes the gap. Eight steps at n = 4, matching B230 × F31.

                                                                                                          Only Bokut–Shiao occurs here. j < j₀ and j₀ + 1 < i force j < j₀ ≤ i − 2 < i − 1, so j ≠ i − 1 and the Yang–Baxter rule never leads on bsWord₁ i j. Unlike §4r, §4u and §4v there is no second instance to discharge — the regime that creates the nesting also rules out the doubling.

                                                                                                          The composition is §4v's, so CyclicFarCommLow.oc and its S-polynomial are reused verbatim; only the chain is new. What is new besides the chain is descWord_split, and that is a word identity the B × B block will want too.

                                                                                                                  §4x Bokut–Shiao against the braid word — the first B × B sub-family #

                                                                                                                  B × B is the last shape, seventeen compositions at n = 4 with chains of nine to twenty-five steps. It is not one family: writing a = i − j₁ and b = i − j₂ for the two depths, the engine's chain lengths depend only on (a, b) and split it up as

                                                                                                                  (1,1) → 8    §4r, the braid self-overlap
(a,1) → 9    this section
(1,2) → 10       (1,3) → 12
(a,2) → 15       (2,3) → 19       (3,3) → 25

                                                                                                                  This section is the column b = 1, i.e. j₂ = i − 1, where the second rule leads on the braid word σᵢσᵢ₋₁σᵢ — six of the seventeen, and the one whose chain is uniform in a.

                                                                                                                  The S-polynomial, in the shape that makes the chain visible. Both rules lead on a word ending in σᵢ, they overlap in that letter, and the ambient word cancels. With E = descWord i−1 j₁, so that descWord i j₁ = σᵢ :: E:

                                                                                                                  spoly = c₂ · ( σᵢ E σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ σᵢ₋₁  −  σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ E σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ )

                                                                                                                  c₂ is the second rule's leading coefficient — 1 for Bokut–Shiao at j = i − 1, −1 for Yang–Baxter, the two rules §4j puts on that word. The first rule cannot be Yang–Baxter: j₁ ≤ i − 2 here, so it leads on a longer word.

                                                                                                                  Both terms reduce to σᵢ₋₂ σᵢ₋₁ σᵢ₋₂ σᵢ E, and every step is one of three rules — Bokut–Shiao at (i−2, i−1, j₁), far-commutation σᵢσᵢ₋₂, and the outer rule itself:

                                                                                                                  term 1 term 2
                                                                                                                  1 BS(i−2,i−1,j₁) at (σᵢ ∣ σᵢσᵢ₋₁) 6 BS(i−2,i−1,j₁) at (σᵢ₋₁σᵢ ∣ σᵢ)
                                                                                                                  2 σᵢσᵢ₋₂ at (ε ∣ E σᵢ σᵢ₋₁) 7 σᵢσᵢ₋₂ at (σᵢ₋₁ ∣ E σᵢ)
                                                                                                                  3 BS(i−1,i,j₁) at (σᵢ₋₂ ∣ σᵢ₋₁) 8 BS(i−1,i,j₁) at (σᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₂ ∣ ε)
                                                                                                                  4 BS(i−2,i−1,j₁) at (σᵢ₋₂σᵢ₋₁σᵢ ∣ ε) 9 BS(i−2,i−1,i−2) at (ε ∣ σᵢ E)
                                                                                                                  5 σᵢσᵢ₋₂ at (σᵢ₋₂σᵢ₋₁ ∣ E)

                                                                                                                  Five steps for the first term, four for the second, nine in all — independent of a, which is why this column is flat where the others grow. The two branches differ only in their last step: term 1 finishes by commuting σᵢ past σᵢ₋₂, term 2 by straightening the braid σᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₂σᵢ₋₁.

                                                                                                                  Every intermediate is told apart by its first letter. The nine stages begin with σᵢ, σᵢ, σᵢ₋₂, σᵢ₋₂, σᵢ₋₂ and σᵢ₋₁, σᵢ₋₁, σᵢ₋₁, σᵢ₋₁ against a passenger beginning with σᵢ₋₁ and then σᵢ₋₂ — so no length count and no word-uniqueness argument is needed anywhere in the section.

                                                                                                                  monicStep is the other thing that keeps this short: every rule the chain applies is monic, every stage is two terms, and the step is always "rewrite the first term, carry the second" — so one lemma discharges all nine.

                                                                                                                  theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.monicStep {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) (r : ReductionRule (HeckeGen n) ℝ) (hr : r ∈ (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp).rules) {L R : Monomial (HeckeGen n)} (hrel : ∀ (w : Monomial (HeckeGen n)), r.relation.coeff w = (AlgElement.ofTerms [(L, 1), (R, -1)]).coeff w) (hlm : r.lm (heckeOrder n) = L) (hLR : R ≠ L) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (a b W W' : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (hW : W = a ++ L ++ b) (hW' : W' = a ++ R ++ b) (hne : ∀ q ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), q ≠ W) :
                                                                                                                  SingleStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (W, c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (W', c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                  One step of a two-term chain, by a monic two-word rule. The stage words are arbitrary and tied to the rule's by equations, so consecutive steps compose without the decompositions having to agree syntactically.

                                                                                                                  §4ah The same, for the quadratic rule #

                                                                                                                  monicStep above asks the rule to be monic with two words, L − R, so that a step is a substitution: one term in, one term out. The quadratic rule σ_z² − h·σ_z − 1 has three, so a step by it is not a substitution — the term (a σ_z² b, c) becomes the pair (a σ_z b, h·c) and (a b, c). That is the whole reason monicStep does not reach the corner's two quadratic steps, and the eight-step chain of §4y writes five of its steps out by hand.

                                                                                                                  quadStep is the missing companion. It is monicStep's statement with the one-term output replaced by the two-term one, and its proof is the same shape: the coefficient at the targeted word is read off by ofTerms_coeff_mid, and the CoeffEq obligation is a split_ifs <;> ring once both sides are unfolded.

                                                                                                                  One lemma covers both occurrences. hecke_quad_pair_shape.py measured the two quadratic steps of the a ≤ b regime and found they apply the same rule, heckeRelation j₁, after the same Yang–Baxter step, differing only in their contexts — the second has σ_{i−2} prepended on the left and lacks a trailing σ_i on the right. Since the contexts here are parameters, that difference costs nothing: the assembly supplies them and the step lemma never sees it.

                                                                                                                  source
                                                                                                                  theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.quadStep {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) (z : Fin n) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (a b W : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (hW : W = a ++ [{ index := z }, { index := z }] ++ b) (hne : ∀ w ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), w ≠ W) :
                                                                                                                  SingleStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (W, c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (a ++ [{ index := z }] ++ b, c * (hp.q - hp.q⁻¹)) :: (a ++ b, c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                  One step of a chain, by the quadratic rule. Unlike monicStep the output has one more term than the input: the quadratic rule has three words, so the targeted term is replaced by two, with coefficients c·(q − q⁻¹) and c.

                                                                                                                  The contexts a, b and the surrounding terms L₁, L₂ are arbitrary, and W is tied to the rule's leading word by an equation rather than being it on the nose, so consecutive steps compose without their decompositions having to agree syntactically — the same reason monicStep is stated that way.

                                                                                                                                          §4y Preparation for the a = 1 row of B × B: transport at any position #

                                                                                                                                          farComm_transport (§4t) moves a generator rightwards but only in an element whose other term is the transport's own destination; farComm_transport_snd / _fst (§4u) add a single bystander. The a = 1 row of B × B needs it with two bystanders and h-weighted coefficients, so here is the rightward transport in the same L₁ ++ (·) :: L₂ form farComm_transport_left (§4v) and monicStep (§4x) already use — the moving term at an arbitrary position of the term list, everything else carried untouched.

                                                                                                                                          With this, all four transports in the file are instances of two lemmas (farComm_transport_left, farComm_transport_right) at arbitrary list positions, and the earlier special cases are only kept because they are already used.

                                                                                                                                          source
                                                                                                                                          theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.farComm_transport_right_sources {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) (x : Fin n) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (w a b : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) :
                                                                                                                                          (∀ y ∈ w, ↑y.index + 1 < ↑x) → (∀ (u v : Monomial (HeckeGen n)), u ++ v = w → v ≠ [] → ∀ r ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), r ≠ a ++ (u ++ { index := x } :: (v ++ b))) → MultiStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (a ++ { index := x } :: (w ++ b), c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (a ++ (w ++ { index := x } :: b), c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                                          Far-commutation transport, rightwards, at any list position. The mirror of farComm_transport_left_sources: there a generator below the block moves left, here a generator above it moves right. The induction recurses on the head of w and prepends its step, the opposite end from the leftward version.

                                                                                                                                          As on the left, the collision hypothesis enumerates the intermediate words by splitting w, and one of those splits names the transport's own final word, which the proof never needs. On this side that split is v = [], not u = [] — the two ends swap with the direction of travel, since here the moving letter starts at the left of w and finishes at its right. Concretely hcol is used at u = [] with v = y :: w for the single step, which is non-empty, and the recursion passes v through untouched.

                                                                                                                                          The distinction matters because the bystanding term of the corner chain is the transport's final word, so the unrestricted hypothesis is false exactly where the transport is needed — the same trap §4v hit on the left, and it would be hit again here by mirroring the wrong end. farComm_transport_right below is this with the stronger hypothesis, kept because §4y's callers already supply it.

                                                                                                                                          source
                                                                                                                                          theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.farComm_transport_right {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) (x : Fin n) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (w a b : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) :
                                                                                                                                          (∀ y ∈ w, ↑y.index + 1 < ↑x) → (∀ (u v : Monomial (HeckeGen n)), u ++ v = w → ∀ r ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), r ≠ a ++ (u ++ { index := x } :: (v ++ b))) → MultiStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (a ++ { index := x } :: (w ++ b), c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (a ++ (w ++ { index := x } :: b), c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                                          The rightward transport with the unrestricted collision hypothesis — every split of w, including the one naming the final word. Weaker than farComm_transport_right_sources and kept for §4y's callers, exactly as farComm_transport_left is kept for §4v's.

                                                                                                                                          §4ai A whole block transported past a run #

                                                                                                                                          The a ≤ b regime's blocks are a levels (or a − 1 on the diagonal), each one letter transported rightwards past a run of far-commutations, and hecke_block_transport_shape.py measures the level lengths as min(b−a−1+k, b−a+2) off the diagonal and min(k, 2) on it. The consequence worth acting on is that the number of short levels is fixed — two, or one on the diagonal — so every remaining level passes the same run descWord (j₁+1) j₂. The block is therefore a fixed prologue followed by a uniform loop, not a nested loop with a growing inner run.

                                                                                                                                          blockTransportRight is that uniform part, and stating it needs no reference to the block at all: it is "carry a whole word X rightwards past a whole word W", by induction peeling X from its right end. Each peel is one farComm_transport_right_sources, and the letter just moved joins B, which is exactly the transition the measurement shows between consecutive levels.

                                                                                                                                          The parked-term hypothesis is loopTwoGen's, and for the same reason. Enumerating the intermediate words here would mean splitting X and W simultaneously, which is unusable in practice. But every word any step of this induction rewrites has the form A ++ z — the accumulator only ever grows to the right of A — so the single hypothesis "no parked term begins with A" discharges every collision obligation at once. In the corner it holds because the two terms start with different letters.

                                                                                                                                          source
                                                                                                                                          theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.blockTransportRightSources {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (A W X B : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) :
                                                                                                                                          (∀ x ∈ X, ∀ y ∈ W, ↑y.index + 1 < ↑x.index) → (∀ (P S u v : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) (x : HeckeGen n), P ++ x :: S = X → u ++ v = W → v ≠ [] → ∀ r ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), r ≠ A ++ (P ++ (u ++ x :: (v ++ (S ++ B))))) → MultiStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (A ++ (X ++ (W ++ B)), c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (A ++ (W ++ (X ++ B)), c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                                          A whole block carried rightwards past a run, with the source-only collision hypothesis. X and W swap, provided every letter of X is at least two above every letter of W, inside any context and at any position of the term list.

                                                                                                                                          The induction peels X from the right: its last letter transports across W first and then joins B, so the recursion re-enters with X one shorter and B one longer. Peeling from the left would not compose — the head of X is separated from W by the rest of X, so no single transport applies.

                                                                                                                                          hpark below — no other term extends A — is sufficient but not necessary, and hecke_prefix_head_separation.py measures where the difference bites: at 2a steps of the corner's closing phase no choice of left context satisfies hpark, while every source in the chain is unique, so the precise condition holds throughout.

                                                                                                                                          What the transport actually needs is that no other term equal a word it rewrites. Peeling X from the right, those are exactly

                                                                                                                                          A ++ P ++ u ++ (x :: (v ++ (S ++ B)))    for  P ++ (x :: S) = X,
                                               u ++ v = W,  v ≠ []

                                                                                                                                          — one per letter of X and per interior split of W. The v ≠ [] exclusion is farComm_transport_right_sources's own (§4ah): it drops the split naming each transport's final word, which is produced and never rewritten. This lemma threads that family through the recursion instead of over-approximating it.

                                                                                                                                          source
                                                                                                                                          theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.blockTransportRight {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (A : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) (hpark : ∀ r ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), ∀ (z : Monomial (HeckeGen n)), r ≠ A ++ z) (W X B : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) :
                                                                                                                                          (∀ x ∈ X, ∀ y ∈ W, ↑y.index + 1 < ↑x.index) → MultiStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (A ++ (X ++ (W ++ B)), c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (A ++ (W ++ (X ++ B)), c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                                          The block transport with the unrestricted hypothesis — hpark supplies every case of the source family at once. Kept because §4aj's callers already supply it, exactly as farComm_transport_right is kept for §4y's.

                                                                                                                                          §4aj The whole block, in three steps #

                                                                                                                                          With blockTransportRight in hand the block closes. The per-level blueprint — measured over 102 levels in hecke_block_transport_shape.py, uniform on and off the diagonal — says the level with high letter σ_h passes descWord (min(h−2, j₁+1)) j₂ and carries descWord (h−1) (j₁+1) ++ [σ_i] on its right. Only two levels sit below the cap, so the block is

                                                                                                                                          h = j₁+1   one transport across `descWord (j₁−1) j₂`
h = j₁+2   one transport across `descWord j₁ j₂`
h ≥ j₁+3   one `blockTransportRight`, `X = descWord i (j₁+3)`

                                                                                                                                          and the two short levels need no lemma of their own — they are farComm_transport_right_sources applications, with the blueprint supplying their arguments.

                                                                                                                                          What makes the three compose is the left contexts, and they are forced. Writing A for the block transport's context, the earlier steps must run at

                                                                                                                                          A₂ = A ++ descWord i (j₁+3) ++ [σ_{j₁+1}]
A₁ = A₂ ++ [σ_{j₁+2}, σ_{j₁}]

                                                                                                                                          and then each step's target is the next one's source on the nose, because descWord j₁ j₂ = σ_{j₁} :: descWord (j₁−1) j₂ and descWord (j₁+1) j₂ = σ_{j₁+1} :: descWord j₁ j₂ peel exactly the letters the contexts carry. Those two descWord_cons peelings and descWord (j₁+2) (j₁+1) = [σ_{j₁+2}, σ_{j₁+1}] are the whole of the gluing.

                                                                                                                                          No bound relating j₁+3 to i is needed. The obvious hypothesis j₁+3 ≤ i is not required and is not taken: if it fails, descWord i (j₁+3) is empty and the middle step is vacuous, which is exactly the degenerate short-block case. Stating it would have narrowed the lemma for nothing.

                                                                                                                                          Two corrections to the first version of this section, both about scope.

                                                                                                                                          The diagonal was excluded. blockPass originally carried hj₂ : j₂ ≤ j₁ − 1, and b = a means j₂ = j₁, so it could not be instantiated there at all — yet a ≤ b includes the diagonal, and the diagonal block is real (a − 1 levels rather than a, starting one level higher). The first level is simply absent there, so the fix is to name the rest: blockPassFromTwo asks only j₂ ≤ j₁ and covers the diagonal, with blockPass = one leading transport + it.

                                                                                                                                          The trailing word was hardcoded. Both versions ended … ++ [σ_i]. That is right for the top-level block, but the same block shape occurs inside the prefix as small(a), where what sits to the right is descWord j₁ j₂ instead. Measured over 131 levels, top-level and small(a) obey one blueprint,

                                                                                                                                          W = descWord (min(h−2, j₁+1)) j_eff        B = descWord (h−1) (j₁+1) ++ T

                                                                                                                                          differing only in j_eff and the tail T. Making T a parameter is what lets one lemma serve both — and small(a) is where the prefix's own block · two steps · block self-similarity stops being an observation and becomes literal reuse.

                                                                                                                                          MultiStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (A ++ (descWord i jppp ++ ([{ index := jp }] ++ { index := jpp } :: (descWord j₁ j₂ ++ ([{ index := jp }] ++ T)))), c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (A ++ (descWord jp j₂ ++ (descWord i jppp ++ (descWord jpp jp ++ T))), c) :: L₂))

Two families, one per underlying transport: the σ_jpp step across descWord j₁ j₂, and the block carried across descWord jp j₂. See blockTransportRightSources (§4ai) for why hpark is stronger than needed.

The trailing word T is a parameter for the same reason — see §4aj.

                                                                                                                                          The block, at general depth, off the diagonal. One pass of the a ≤ b regime's far-commutation block when j₂ < j₁: the first level below the cap, then blockPassFromTwo for the rest.

                                                                                                                                          The left context A and the trailing word T are both arbitrary — the block never has to know what the prefix left on either side of it.

                                                                                                                                          §4al The quadratic pair, at general depth #

                                                                                                                                          The prefix uses the quadratic rule exactly twice, and each time the step before it is a Yang–Baxter. hecke_quad_pair_shape.py measured both occurrences and they differ only in their surrounding words, so one lemma covers them — but the mechanism is worth stating, because it is what makes the pair a pair rather than two unrelated steps:

                                                                                                                                          L ++ [σ_{j₁+1}, σ_{j₁}, σ_{j₁+1}] ++ (σ_{j₁} :: R)
  Y →   L ++ [σ_{j₁}, σ_{j₁+1}] ++ [σ_{j₁}, σ_{j₁}] ++ R
  Q →   (L ++ [σ_{j₁}, σ_{j₁+1}, σ_{j₁}] ++ R,  c·h)
        (L ++ [σ_{j₁}, σ_{j₁+1}] ++ R,          c)

                                                                                                                                          The Yang–Baxter step ends by emitting a σ_{j₁}, and R already begins with one. The two land adjacent, and that is the quadratic redex. Neither step creates it alone.

                                                                                                                                          The Yang–Baxter step does not go through yangBaxterRelation. That rule carries −1 at its own leading word, so it is not monic and monicStep cannot take it. The route is bokutShiaoRelation j₁ (j₁+1) j₁, which is the same relation at j = i − 1 (§4j) but monic and with the leading word the right way round — braid_hrel / braid_hlm are exactly that repackaging.

                                                                                                                                          source
                                                                                                                                          theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.quadPair {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hp : HeckeParams) {j₁ jp : Fin n} (hjp : ↑j₁ + 1 = ↑jp) (c : ℝ) (hc : c ≠ 0) (L₁ L₂ : List (Monomial (HeckeGen n) × ℝ)) (L R : Monomial (HeckeGen n)) (hpark : ∀ r ∈ List.map Prod.fst (L₁ ++ L₂), ∀ (z : Monomial (HeckeGen n)), r ≠ L ++ z) :
                                                                                                                                          MultiStepReduction (heckeOrder n) (heckeCompletedRewritingSystem n hn hp) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (L ++ ([{ index := jp }, { index := j₁ }, { index := jp }] ++ { index := j₁ } :: R), c) :: L₂)) (AlgElement.ofTerms (L₁ ++ (L ++ ([{ index := j₁ }, { index := jp }] ++ { index := j₁ } :: R), c * (hp.q - hp.q⁻¹)) :: (L ++ ([{ index := j₁ }, { index := jp }] ++ R), c) :: L₂))

                                                                                                                                          The Yang–Baxter step and the quadratic step it sets up. One term in, two out, with the h-weighted one first. L and R are arbitrary: the pair occurs twice in the prefix and the two occurrences differ only in them.

                                                                                                                                          theorem UGB.GrobnerShirshov.Hecke.descWord_head {n : ℕ} {i j : Fin n} (hj : ↑j ≤ ↑i) :
                                                                                                                                          ∃ (t : List (HeckeGen n)), descWord i j = { index := i } :: t

                                                                                                                                          The descending run begins with its top index, whenever it is non-empty. Splits on j = i (descWord_self) and j < i (descWord_cons at i − 1).

                                                                                                                                          The words #

                                                                                                                                          Thirteen of them, all over the common tail T = descWord i−2 j₂. Their lengths are what separates them at almost every step: t+5, t+4, t+3, t+2, t+1 with only three collisions, resolved by a first or fourth letter.

                                                                                                                                                                                              The eight fixed steps #

                                                                                                                                                                                              Five of them apply the quadratic rule, which has three words, so monicStep (§4x) does not reach them and each is written out.                                                                                                                                                                                               Bokut–Shiao at j = i − 1 against it.

                                                                                                                                                                                              §4z Both depths at i − 2 — the first corner case of B × B #

                                                                                                                                                                                              The five that remain after §4x and §4y all have a, b ≥ 2: both rules at general depth, neither on the braid word. This is the corner a = b = 2, i.e. j₁ = j₂ = i − 2, where the composition is a Bokut–Shiao rule against itself at a proper overlap — the analogue of §4r one level down.

                                                                                                                                                                                              Because a, b ≥ 2 puts both leading monomials strictly longer than the braid word, neither rule can be Yang–Baxter: there is no §4j doubling here, and the family is one composition per i rather than four. At n = 4 that is B120 × B120 and B231 × B231.

                                                                                                                                                                                              Everything is explicit. With x = σᵢ, y = σᵢ₋₁, z = σᵢ₋₂, both depths pinned at i − 2 make descWord i j₁ = xyz and descWord i−1 j₂ = yz, so every word in the chain is a literal five-, six- or seven-letter list in three generators. The S-polynomial is

                                                                                                                                                                                              spoly = x y z y x y z  −  y x y z y z x

                                                                                                                                                                                              and the chain is fifteen steps. Thirteen of them apply a two-word monic rule — the braid rule at (i−2, i−1), the braid rule at (i−1, i), far-commutation σᵢσᵢ₋₂, and the rule itself — so monicStep (§4x) discharges each in a few lines. Only steps 4 and 7 are quadratic, and those are written out.

                                                                                                                                                                                              The two quadratic steps are where h enters, and it leaves again at step 11: z y x z y z and z y z x y z both carry h there with opposite signs and cancel, taking the element from four live terms back to two. The h-weighted pair is kept in the term list rather than merged, because monicStep produces the unmerged list and a merge would need its own step; carrying it costs nothing since the surviving stages are still told apart by length or third letter.

                                                                                                                                                                                              No transports. Unlike §4y this corner needs none: with both depths at i − 2 there is no run left to cross, which is exactly why it is the corner to do first. The remaining three — (3,2), (2,3), (3,3) at 15, 19 and 25 steps — reintroduce the runs and with them the transports.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Fifteen steps, to zero.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  §4aa Depths i−3 and i−2 — the unequal corner, and the cheapest of the three #

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Of the three that remain after §4z this is the one to take next, because nothing in it is quadratic: all fifteen steps apply a two-word monic rule and every stage has exactly two terms, so monicStep discharges the whole chain and h never appears. (a, b) = (3, 2), i.e. j₁ = i − 3 and j₂ = i − 2.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Writing x = σᵢ, y = σᵢ₋₁, z = σᵢ₋₂, w = σᵢ₋₃, both depths are pinned, so descWord i j₁ = xyzw and descWord i−1 j₂ = yz and every word is an explicit eight-letter list in four generators:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  spoly = x y z w y x y z  −  y x y z w y z x

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Seven steps take the second term to z y z w x y z w, eight take the first to the same word, and they cancel. Six rules occur — the Bokut–Shiao rule at (i−2,i−1,i−3), the braid rule at (i−3,i−2), the three far-commutations σᵢσᵢ₋₂, σᵢσᵢ₋₃, σᵢ₋₁σᵢ₋₃, and the composition's own first rule.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Why the count is 15 and not less. Reducing the two terms separately to normal form takes 8 and 7 steps, and 8 + 7 = 15 — the chain is exactly the two reductions, with no shared intermediate to cut. That holds for all four corner cases ((2,2): 7+8=15, (2,3): 9+10=19, (3,3): 12+13=25), so there is no shorter route to be found by looking for a common midpoint; an earlier guess that one existed was wrong.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Every distinctness is a first, second, third or fourth letter among four generators.
